title: Hezekiah's Illness, Tears, and Song
summary: Isaiah tells Hezekiah that he is about to die, but the king prays and weeps, and God answers through the prophet with fifteen more years, a promise to defend Jerusalem, and a sign: the shadow on the stairway of Ahaz goes back ten steps. Hezekiah then writes a psalm about facing death and being brought back from the edge of the grave. Two closing verses add the remedy Isaiah prescribed and the king's request for a sign.
story: Chapter 37 showed Hezekiah praying for his city; chapter 38 shows him praying for his life. The deliverance of Jerusalem and the healing of the king are tied together in verse 6, and both are gifts to a king who turns to God. Yet this chapter also prepares for the next one. A man granted fifteen years is still a mortal man, and in chapter 39 he will use his restored health to show off his treasures to envoys from Babylon. The pair of chapters forms the hinge of the whole book: the Assyrian crisis ends, the Babylonian future comes into view, and chapter 40 will speak to a people in exile.
historical:
“In those days” is a loose time marker, and the chapter's place in the book is probably thematic rather than chronological. Hezekiah is usually dated to about 715 to 686 BC (some chronologies place his reign earlier), so fifteen added years would put the illness around 701 BC, the year of Sennacherib's invasion, which fits the promise in verse 6 that the city will be delivered from the king of Assyria. The Babylonian embassy of chapter 39 came from Merodach-baladan, who held Babylon twice against Assyria, and many historians think his overture to Hezekiah fits best before the 701 campaign, when he was gathering allies for revolt. On that reading, chapters 38 and 39 step back in time, and the editor has placed them after the Assyrian story so that the book can turn toward Babylon.

The “stairway of Ahaz” was presumably built by Hezekiah's father. Whether it was designed as a sundial or was simply a staircase whose shadow marked the time of day is unknown. The parallel account in 2 Kings 20:1-11 tells the same events in a different order and includes Hezekiah's choice of whether the shadow should go forward or back.
cultural:
Turning his face to the wall gave the sick king privacy in a room that was likely full of attendants, and it signaled that his appeal was to God alone. The instruction to set his house in order meant making arrangements for succession and property, which carried extra weight for a king who, on the chronology of 2 Kings 21:1, did not yet have his heir Manasseh.

Hezekiah's psalm reflects Israel's common view of death in this period. Sheol, the realm of the dead, was pictured as a place of silence and shadow, far from the worship of the temple. “Sheol cannot thank You; Death cannot praise You.” The dead were not thought to cease entirely, but they were cut off from the praise and fellowship that made life life. That is why the psalm treats rescue from death as rescue for worship. The images of the psalm come from ordinary life: a shepherd's tent taken down, a weaver cutting a finished length of cloth off the loom, the thin cries of birds. The remedy in verse 21, a lump of pressed figs applied to a boil, was a plain household treatment, and the text sees no conflict between using it and receiving healing from God.
literary: The chapter has three parts. A prose narrative (verses 1 to 8) moves from death sentence, to prayer, to reprieve and sign. A poem (verses 9 to 20), introduced as “a writing by Hezekiah,” follows the shape of a psalm of thanksgiving: the speaker recalls his distress in the first person (verses 10 to 14), turns on the question “What can I say?” (verse 15), and ends in praise and a vow to sing in the house of the LORD. The poem appears only in Isaiah, not in 2 Kings. Verses 21 and 22 read like an appendix: in 2 Kings 20:7-8 the fig remedy and the request for a sign come before the sign is given. Here they are placed at the end, and Hezekiah's last question, about going up to the house of the LORD, echoes the final line of his song.

doctrines.note: God's answer is personal: “I have heard your prayer; I have seen your tears.” The chapter presents prayer as something that genuinely matters in God's dealings with his people, not a formality that changes nothing.
God heals through a sign and through a poultice of figs. The chapter holds the extraordinary and the ordinary together as means in the hand of the same God.

Hezekiah's view of death is bleak, and the chapter lets it stand. Later Scripture, including Isaiah itself (25:8; 26:19), speaks of God swallowing up death and raising the dead, and that fuller hope grows out of prayers like this one.

words.note: Sheol, the realm of the dead. In the Old Testament it is where all the dead go, righteous and wicked alike, often described as below, dark, and silent. It is not the same as the later idea of hell as a place of punishment, though older translations sometimes render it that way. Hezekiah fears going through its gates “in the prime of my life.”

Emet, faithfulness or truth. Hezekiah claims he walked before God “faithfully” (verse 3), and the psalm twice celebrates God's own faithfulness (verses 18 and 19). The word describes reliability, the quality of someone whose word holds. The king's appeal and his praise meet in it.

Yadah, to give thanks or praise, often in public acknowledgment of what God has done. The psalm's logic hangs on it: the dead cannot give thanks, but “the living, only the living, can thank You.” Restored life is life given back for thanksgiving.

Ot, sign. Both halves of the story turn on signs, one offered by God (verse 7) and one asked for by Hezekiah (verse 22). The contrast with Hezekiah's father is deliberate: Ahaz refused a sign in chapter 7, while his son receives one.

christ: The chapter connects to Christ thematically, through its concern with death. Hezekiah, a son of David, is sentenced to die, weeps and prays, and is brought back from the edge of the grave; according to 2 Kings 20:5 he would go up to the house of the LORD on the third day. The New Testament tells of a greater son of David who also prayed with tears to the one who could save him from death (Hebrews 5:7), yet was not spared dying, and was raised on the third day. Hezekiah's rescue bought fifteen years. Christ's resurrection is presented as the defeat of death itself, the answer to the fear voiced in this psalm that the grave is a place where no one can praise God. The parallels are ones a reader can see from the far side of Easter, not predictions within the chapter.

hard.q: God announced that Hezekiah would die and then gave him fifteen more years. Did God change his mind?
hard.a:
Read on its surface, the chapter shows God declaring one outcome and then, after prayer, granting another. Christians have explained this in more than one way. Many hold that prophetic warnings of judgment often carry an unstated condition, as Jeremiah 18:7-10 says outright and as the story of Nineveh in Jonah shows: God announces what will happen if nothing changes, precisely so that people will turn to him. On this view God's purpose was constant, and the prayer was part of how it came about. Others, especially those who stress God's real relationship with people in time, take the text to mean that God genuinely responds to prayer and alters what he does. Both readings agree on what the chapter wants its readers to see: Hezekiah's prayer was heard, and God's answer was an act of mercy rather than a reversal of his character.

A second difficulty is the sign itself, a shadow moving backward. Some take it as a local miracle affecting the light at that stairway, others as a larger event. The text is interested in what it signified, not in the mechanism, and it leaves the mechanism unexplained.

questions: Hezekiah turned his face to the wall and wept. What does his honesty in prayer suggest about how we can speak to God in fear or grief?
The psalm says the living can thank God in a way the dead cannot. How might knowing that your days are numbered change what you do with the years you have?
God healed Hezekiah through both a sign and a poultice of figs. Why do you think people sometimes treat medical care and prayer as rivals?
